paras: The killing of Robert Good, also reported as John Goodwin, was the shooting death of a Black man by pursuing white citizens near McGehee, Arkansas, on 3 July 1903, hours after he was accused of firing the shot that killed railway conductor B. L. Wright. Wire reports said a posse killed him while he resisted arrest, but the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic, citing sheriff's officers, said two unidentified men ambushed him with shotguns before any officer arrived. No arrest was reported, and the story ran widely in white papers as the killing of a conductor by a 'boisterous negro'.

Wright was a passenger conductor on the Iron Mountain road who had been on the division about four months. On the afternoon of 3 July he was riding with his wife and children toward Little Rock to spend the Fourth. According to the Graphic, a Black man named Goodwin boarded near McGhee, became noisy, and was told by the porter to keep quiet or be put off the train.

The Arkansas Gazette's McGehee correspondent wrote that the passenger was scuffling with the porter, George Davis, when Davis drew a gun, and that the passenger took it and fired at close range. The bullet passed through the glass door of the coach and the wooden door of the baggage car and struck Wright in the neck, and he died in his wife's arms. A passenger forced the man to give up the gun at gunpoint, and he ran down the railroad as several shots were fired after him. The train was held at McGehee for an inquest, which returned a verdict that Wright was murdered by Robert Good.

That evening a Pine Bluff correspondent reported that 'All Southeast Arkansas' was aroused and that the fugitive 'may be lynched' if captured. Sheriff Gould, deputies Philpot, Dunlap and Tom Meeks, and the county bloodhounds left Pine Bluff at about 6 o'clock on a special train. By then, according to the officers, two McGhee men armed with double-barrel shotguns had waited near the man's home and, after dark, fired four charges of buckshot into him. The Gazette special instead said that 'a score of posses' had cornered him late in the afternoon and shot him to death while he resisted arrest.

The officers returned to Pine Bluff saying they could not learn who the two men were. A telegram from Monticello to the Graphic named the killer as Hugh Henry and said the man had resisted arrest. No report of an inquest into the Black man's death, of any arrest, or of a grand jury inquiry was found. Wright's body was prepared for burial at Little Rock and sent to Fort Smith for interment.

The Associated Press version, credited to a special to the Arkansas Gazette, appeared on 4 and 5 July in papers in Montgomery, Richmond, Savannah, Omaha and Raleigh. It called Wright's death accidental, described the accused as 'a boisterous negro passenger', and stated as fact that he was killed while resisting arrest. Headlines included 'BAD ROBERT GOOD.' in the Montgomery Advertiser, 'Posse Overtook and Slew His Negro Slayer' in the Savannah Morning News, and 'Negro Killed for Shooting Passenger' in the Raleigh News & Observer.

Arkansas papers gave the name as John Goodwin, and the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic placed the killings among four Fourth of July 'tragedies' in and around Pine Bluff. Only the Graphic described the killing as an ambush by private citizens, printing the officers' admission that the men were unknown beside a telegram repeating the resisting-arrest version. A state-news digest carried by Arkansas weeklies through mid-July headed the item 'Conductor Wright Killed by a Stray Bullet Fired by a Drunken Negro' and called the accused 'the murderer'. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

The accounts disagree on the man's name, on whether the pistol was the porter's or his own, and on whether Wright was hit while interrupting a quarrel or by a stray shot; they also differ on whether a posse or two men in ambush killed the accused. The ambush version comes from the sheriff's party that went to the scene, while the resisting-arrest versions do not name their source.

reader.title: Killing of Robert Good (John Goodwin)
bases: The accused Black man was hunted down and shot dead the same day by pursuing citizens, described as a posse in the wire and digest (A1, A7, A10) and as two unidentified armed men lying in wait in the local Pine Bluff account (A9), before sheriff's officers arrived.

He was killed without arrest or trial in retaliation for the shooting of conductor Wright (A7, A9); the wire's claim that a posse killed him 'while resisting arrest' (A1, A10) comes only from the pursuers' side, while the Pine Bluff Graphic, citing returning officers, describes two unidentified men ambushing him with shotguns before any officer arrived (A9), so both the legality and the size of the group are unsettled.

The Arkansas Gazette special (A1, A7), the Pine Bluff Graphic (A8, A9) and the state digest (A10) independently report that the Black man accused of killing Wright was shot to death by pursuers on the day of the shooting, though they differ on his name and on how he was killed.

accounts.label: Arkansas Gazette special (wire)
accounts.gist: Good took the porter's revolver and fired; he escaped but was overtaken by a posse, or cornered by 'a score of posses' late in the afternoon, and killed while resisting arrest.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff officers' report
accounts.gist: Two McGhee men with shotguns waited near Goodwin's home and killed him with four charges of buckshot after dark; officers arriving by special train were too late and could not learn the men's names.

accounts.label: Monticello telegram
accounts.gist: The man who killed Wright 'resisted arrest and was killed by Hugh Henry'.

accounts.label: Arkansas state-news digest
accounts.gist: Goodwin drew a pistol that went off when the porter grappled with him; a posse found him in a house four miles from McGehee and shot him when he refused to surrender.

framing.detail: The Associated Press version ran under headlines such as 'BAD ROBERT GOOD.', 'White Man Killed by Boisterous Negro', 'Posse Overtook and Slew His Negro Slayer' and 'Negro Killed for Shooting Passenger', repeating that he was killed 'while resisting arrest'.
The Bryan Morning Eagle's 'Tragedy on a Train' stressed the 'Innocent Man Dead' and the accidental nature of the shot.
The St. Louis Republic's 'Conductor Shot Down by a Negro Man' anticipated that he 'may be lynched'; the Pine Bluff Graphic told the ambush in plain terms as one of four Fourth of July 'tragedies'.
The Arkansas digest headline blamed 'a Drunken Negro' and called him 'the murderer' while describing the shot as accidental.

conflicts.note: Both names describe the same man; the Pine Bluff and digest reports are closer to the scene, the Gazette special came from McGehee itself.

info: Friday, 3 July 1903: Wright shot about 3 or 3:30 p.m.; the accused killed late that afternoon (A7) or after dark (A9).
Shooting on an Iron Mountain passenger train entering McGehee (McGhee), Arkansas; the accused was killed near his home (A9) or in a house about four miles from McGehee (A10).
One Black man, called 'Robert Good' in the Arkansas Gazette special and 'John Goodwin' in the Pine Bluff reports and state digest.
Accused of shooting and killing conductor B. L. Wright on the train during a scuffle with the porter over a pistol; an inquest at McGehee found Wright 'murdered by Robert Good'.
A posse (wire, digest); two unidentified citizens of McGhee with double-barrel shotguns (Pine Bluff Graphic, from officers' report); 'Hugh Henry' (Monticello telegram to the Graphic).
